nameStory: Korean cornel dogwood gets its name from its native range in Korea (and also China and Japan, despite sometimes being called Japanese cornel). The "cornel" part refers to its relationship to the cornelian cherry dogwoods, whose extremely hard wood was once used to make spear points and tool handles - the name comes from the Latin "cornu" meaning horn, referring to this horn-like hardness.
description: Korean cornel dogwood is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree or large shrub in the dogwood family. It typically grows 15-25 feet tall with an upright, somewhat vase-shaped form. Like other dogwoods, it has distinctive oval leaves with curved parallel veins, but this Asian species is quite rare in New England landscapes. It produces small yellowish flowers in early spring before the leaves emerge, followed by bright red oval fruits in late summer.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stems, with the characteristic dogwood feature of curved parallel veins that arc toward the leaf tip. The leaves feel smooth and have a slightly glossy surface.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow to greenish-yellow flowers appear in early spring before leaves emerge, clustered in small rounded groups. Each tiny flower has four petals and lacks the showy white bracts of flowering dogwood.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red, oval-shaped drupes (cherry-like fruits) about half an inch long ripen in late summer. The fruits have a somewhat glossy skin and contain a single hard seed inside.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray-brown bark that becomes somewhat furrowed and scaly with age. On younger branches, the bark feels smooth and has a grayish color with subtle texture.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a small tree or large shrub with an upright, somewhat vase-shaped form. Branches tend to grow in an opposite pattern, creating a fairly regular branching structure.

habitat: Korean cornel dogwood is extremely rare in New England, found only as an occasional ornamental planting in parks, botanical gardens, or residential landscapes. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. Since it's not native to the region, you won't find it growing wild in natural areas.

seasonality.spring: Small yellow flowers bloom in early spring before the leaves emerge, making it one of the earlier dogwoods to flower. New leaves unfurl shortly after flowering, appearing bright green.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage displays the characteristic opposite, oval leaves with curved parallel veins. Young fruits begin developing and gradually enlarge through the season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn reddish or purplish before dropping. The bright red oval fruits ripen and become quite conspicuous, often persisting into early winter.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the opposite branching pattern typical of dogwoods. Some red fruits may persist on the tree, and the gray-brown bark becomes more visible.

funFact: Despite being called "Korean cornel dogwood" and sometimes "Japanese cornelian cherry," this tree produces fruits that are actually edible and have been used in traditional Asian medicine for over 2,000 years - the species name "officinalis" literally means "of the pharmacy" because of its medicinal uses!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with cornelian cherry dogwood (Cornus mas), which also has early yellow flowers and red fruits. Korean cornel dogwood has more oval-shaped fruits compared to the rounder fruits of cornelian cherry, and its leaves tend to be slightly more pointed. Both are rare in New England, so any early-flowering dogwood with yellow blooms and red fruits deserves a closer look.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name "cherry" fool you - this isn't related to true cherries (Prunus species) at all, but gets the name because its red fruits somewhat resemble cherries. The "Korean" in the name is somewhat misleading too, as it's native to China and Japan as well as Korea, and is sometimes called Japanese cornel instead.
compareHints: Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries. Unlike flowering dogwood and kousa dogwood, it lacks the showy white petal-like bracts, and unlike the shrubby dogwoods like red osier or silky dogwood, it grows as a small tree with a more upright form.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.
